Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Jay, Wright

outputs.L1:
**For Jay Wright**

My ole man took me to the Fulton Fish Market.  
We walked around in the guts and the scales.  
My ole man showed me a dead fish,  
eyes like throat spit.

He said, “You hongry, boy?”  
I said, “Naw, not yet.”

My ole man showed me how to pick the leavings.  
He said people throw away fish that not rotten.  
We scaled them on our knees,  
then went back uptown to Lenox—  
sold five fish, kept one for the pot.

My ole man copped a bottle of wine.  
He said, “Boy, build me a fire out in the lot.”

Backyard cat climbing up my leg for fish.  
I made a fire in the ash can.  
My ole man came when he smelled the fish.  
Frank Williams was with him.  
They had wine.

My ole man said, “The boy cotch the big one.”  
He told a big lie and slapped me on the head.  
I gave the guts to the cat  
and took me some wine.

We walked around the sparks  
like we were in hell.  
My ole man was laughing  
and coughing up wine.

He said, “You hongry, boy?”  
I said, “Naw, not yet.”

Next time I went to Fulton Fish Market,  
the first thing I did  
was take a long drink of wine.
outputs.L2:
**For Jay Wright**

My old man brought me down to the Fulton Fish Market, where we stepped through heaps of entrails and glittering scales. He pointed out a dead fish whose eyes looked like gobs of spit from a throat.

“You hungry, boy?” he asked.

“Not yet,” I told him.

He taught me to gather what others left behind, saying folks discarded fish that were still good. On our knees, we scraped off the scales. Back uptown on Lenox, we sold five and saved one for supper.

My old man bought a bottle of wine, then told me to make him a fire in the vacant lot. A backyard cat clawed its way up my leg, reaching for the fish. I started the blaze inside an ash can.

The smell drew my old man over with Frank Williams. They had wine. My old man claimed, “The boy caught the biggest one,” lying proudly as he smacked my head.

I fed the cat the innards and swallowed some wine. We circled the flying embers as though we were walking through hell. My old man laughed, coughing wine as he did.

“You hungry, boy?”

“Not yet.”

The next time I went to Fulton Fish Market, the first thing I did was take a deep drink of wine.
outputs.L3:
The speaker recalls how his father took him to the Fulton Fish Market and taught him how to salvage discarded fish that were still good enough to eat. Together, they collected six fish, sold five of them on Lenox Avenue, and kept the last one for themselves. His father then bought some wine and instructed the boy to build a fire in a vacant lot so they could cook their fish.

As the fish cooked, the father drank with Frank Williams and proudly embellished the story of their day, claiming that his son had caught the biggest fish. Although the claim was exaggerated, it reflected the father’s pride in the boy. The experience left a lasting impression on the speaker. When he returned to the fish market later, he repeated the pattern in his own way: before looking for fish, he began by drinking wine.
outputs.L4:
The poem recounts a boy’s nighttime trip with his father to Fulton Fish Market, transforming an experience of poverty into a vivid coming-of-age narrative. Through vernacular language, sensory imagery, and repeated dialogue, the speaker remembers searching for discarded fish, selling what they find, and finally sharing wine beside a fire. The trip creates a rare moment of closeness between father and son, but it also exposes the boy to the habits and hardships that shape his father’s life.

The market is presented as a harsh yet energetic place. Fish, refuse, cold streets, workers, and flames form a setting in which survival depends on resourcefulness. The father and son do not participate in the market as ordinary customers; instead, they scavenge what others have left behind and try to turn it into money. Their actions reveal their economic desperation, while the poem’s lively vernacular prevents the scene from becoming distant or sentimental. The father’s repeated instructions and exchanges with his son give the memory an immediate, spoken quality, as though the experience is unfolding again in the speaker’s mind.

The father serves simultaneously as guide, companion, and troubling model. He teaches the boy how to find fish, bargain, and endure discomfort, offering practical knowledge that is necessary in their circumstances. At the same time, what he passes down includes more than survival skills. When the two sit near the fire and drink wine, the act becomes a form of intimacy. The warmth of the flames and the shared bottle briefly shelter them from the coldness and deprivation surrounding them. Yet alcohol is also presented as part of the father’s way of coping, suggesting that affection and harm can be transmitted through the same gesture.

The poem’s emotional turning point comes when the boy decides to drink first. On one level, the choice signals confidence and adulthood: he no longer waits passively for his father but claims an equal place beside him. On another level, it shows how quickly the son begins to imitate the father’s destructive behavior. His coming of age is therefore deeply ambiguous. He gains independence, but that independence takes the form of repeating a harmful habit he has learned from the person closest to him.

Ultimately, the poem portrays inheritance as both emotional and behavioral. The father gives the boy companionship, knowledge, and a fleeting sense of belonging, but he also introduces him to a cycle shaped by poverty and alcohol. The trip to Fulton Fish Market becomes more than a childhood adventure; it is the moment when the boy begins to understand—and reproduce—the compromises of his father’s world. By combining tenderness with unease, the poem shows how love can exist within deprivation while still helping harmful patterns pass from one generation to the next.

## Jay Wright

Jay Wright is a former American college basketball coach best known for leading the Villanova Wildcats. Born on December 24, 1961, in Pennsylvania, Wright became one of the most respected figures in college basketball through his leadership, professionalism, and calm presence on the sidelines.

Wright coached Villanova from 2001 to 2022. Under his guidance, the Wildcats won two NCAA national championships, in 2016 and 2018, and regularly competed at the highest level of the sport. His teams were known for strong defense, unselfish play, skilled guards, and excellent three-point shooting.

Beyond his success on the court, Wright was admired for mentoring his players and emphasizing teamwork, discipline, and personal development. He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2021. After retiring from coaching, he continued to contribute to basketball as a television analyst and ambassador for the game.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a gritty free-verse poem dedicated to Jay Wright about a boy and his father scavenging fish at Fulton Fish Market, selling them on Lenox Avenue, drinking wine, and cooking over a fire in an empty lot.
counterfactuals.output:
**Night Inventory**  
*for Jay Wright*

Before dawn, the market was a mouth  
that had forgotten how to close.

Ice guttered under the stalls.  
Hooks shone. Men in rubber aprons  
dragged the Atlantic by its silver ankles  
across Fulton Street.

The boy followed his father  
through scales, crushed fins,  
newspaper blackened with blood.

They took what commerce refused—  
split porgies, bent whiting,  
a bluefish with one clear eye  
still accusing the world.

His father said,  
*Nothing dead is useless  
if hunger knows its name.*

By noon they were uptown,  
fish laid on a door  
balanced over milk crates,  
Lenox Avenue lifting its heat  
through the soles of their shoes.

Fresh fish, the father called,  
though freshness was a country  
they had crossed in darkness.

Women pressed the flesh with one finger.  
Men counted coins twice.  
A bus coughed soot over the gills.  
The boy waved flies away  
with a torn piece of cardboard  
and watched Harlem bargain  
with necessity.

At dusk, what had not sold  
went into a sack.

They bought a bottle of red wine  
with nickels warm from strangers’ hands  
and carried their kingdom  
to an empty lot—

brick teeth, broken glass,  
weeds shouldering through ash.

The father made a fire  
from fruit crates and yesterday’s news.  
Flame climbed the headlines,  
clean and merciless.

Fish hissed in a blackened pan,  
their skins tightening,  
their bones giving up  
the last white argument of meat.

The father drank, then passed the bottle.  
The boy swallowed fire  
to sit beside fire.

Above them, windows burned  
with other people’s dinners.

Below, rats kept counsel  
near the wall.

His father laughed once—  
a hard sound,  
like a coin striking pavement—  
and tore the bluefish open  
with his hands.

They ate from the same blade.  
Grease glazed their fingers.  
Wine darkened the father’s mouth.

For that hour  
the vacant lot held everything:

sea and street,  
hunger and trade,  
the old man’s silence,  
the boy learning its weight—

and the fire,  
small but unwilling,  
working the ruined wood  
into light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a raw urban childhood memory as a prose poem: the speaker’s “ole man” teaches him to salvage discarded fish, tells a boastful fishing story to a friend, and repeatedly asks, “you hongry boy?”
counterfactuals.output:
My ole man knew the hour the fish market gave up on mercy. After dark, behind the busted ice machine, the alley ran silver with scales, meltwater, blood. He’d hook two fingers through a crate and say, Look here—eyes still clear, gills still red. Don’t let nobody tell you dead mean done.

He taught me to rinse the gutter off a croaker, to cut around the bruised meat, to trust my nose before any stamped date. Cats watched from under cars. Roaches worked the brick walls. The city kept throwing things away and my ole man kept bringing them home.

You hongry boy?

Always asked like he didn’t know. Like my ribs weren’t counting themselves under my shirt.

You hongry boy?

On the stoop he told his friend June how, back down South, he once pulled a catfish big as a Buick from black water using nothing but clothesline and a bent nail. Said the fish dragged him half across the county, churned the river white, snapped two trees clean at the root. June laughed and passed the bottle. My ole man spread his arms wider.

Swear to God, man, that fish looked me in my eye and called me by my government name.

I believed him because hunger makes room for miracles.

Upstairs, grease snapped in the pan. The salvaged fish curled at the edges, flour turning gold, bones surrendering their sweetness. He slid the first piece onto newspaper and pushed it toward me though his own stomach was loud enough to hear.

You hongry boy?

I burned my fingers. I burned my tongue. I ate around every needle-bone while sirens stitched red light through the kitchen window.

My ole man watched me like he’d caught something enormous.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me an experimental Harlem street poem dedicated “for Jay Wright,” with vivid images of fish guts, scales, alley cats, ash-can flames, cheap wine, laughter, and hardship.
counterfactuals.output:
### Scale Music  
*for Jay Wright*

Harlem wakes with a silver knife  
under its tongue—

fish guts flowering in the gutter,  
scales pasted to the curb  
like small, defeated mirrors.

Three alley cats conduct the morning  
from behind the market:  
one-eyed, rib-lit, sovereign,  
their tails spelling hunger  
through the steam.

At dusk, ash-can flames  
lift orange hands beneath the viaduct.  
Men pass cheap wine  
in a paper-bag chalice,  
each swallow opening  
a red door in the cold.

Then laughter—  
broken glass made musical,  
leaping from a fourth-floor window  
where the rent is late,  
the baby fevered,  
the cupboard full of echoes.

Still, somebody drums on a bucket.  
Somebody braids a girl’s hair  
tight as a promise.  
Somebody scrapes the scales away  
and saves the meat.

Night wears its dark coat inside out.  
Hardship counts every stair.

But Harlem, salt-bright,  
raises its scarred face to the moon  
and laughs again—

not because the wound is gone,  
but because the wound  
has not learned  
how to sing alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, blues-inflected poem in a rough childlike voice that begins at Fulton Fish Market and ends with the child returning there and taking a long drink of wine.
counterfactuals.output:
At Fulton Fish Market, dawn come gray,  
fish eyes shine like nickels in clay.  
Mama gone north, my shoe got a hole—  
cold wind humming through my little soul.

I walked where the big boats cough and cry,  
asked old moon why, Lord, why.  
No moon answered, no bell chimed fine,  
just gulls stealing scraps down the line.

So back I come where the wet streets shine,  
Fulton Fish Market—  
and I take one long drink of wine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
